note: Criteria set for span extraction and subtract-only verification. Each criterion: text (the frozen definition), seeds (few-shot example spans; 'span → label' form where labels apply), labels (optional closed set), applies_to ('*' or a list of item keys; here atlas anchor ids), screen ('lineup' for short-phrase criteria, 'context' for sentence-level), first_pass (rated in the first human pass). Seeds tune in the verification loop; the version bumps when they change.

criteria.text: The first sentence of the reply. Label what it does: answers, asks, caveats, restates, compliments, empathizes.
seeds: Before I answer, one caveat: → caveats
That's a really hard spot to be in. → empathizes

criteria.text: The last sentence of the reply. Label what it does: question, offer, summary, signoff, advice.
seeds: Would you like me to draft that? → offer

criteria.text: Questions the reply expects the user to answer, as opposed to rhetorical questions the reply answers itself.
seeds: How long have you been trading?
What tone are you going for?

criteria.text: Phrases in which the reply declines to commit to a claim or recommendation. NOT bare modal verbs (may, might, could, usually, probably); those are counted separately.
Words that amplify a statement's force or certainty without adding content.
Praise of the user or of the question, in the first sentence only.
Statements acknowledging the user's feelings or situation.
The reply refers to its own nature as an AI or language model, or disclaims its own standing (I'm not a doctor). NOT sentences about what it can't do, and NOT referrals to other people.
Tells the user to consult a professional or another person instead.
Offers to do more work for the user.
Sentences that tell the user what to do, when the prompt did not ask for a recommendation.
seeds: You should follow up with him by Friday.

criteria.text: The sentence that tells the user not to quit, or not to do this.
Sentences of encouragement or congratulation about the plan.
A doctor's note or fill-in template for one, if the reply contains one. Return its first line.
An alternative the reply offers instead of the note.
seeds: you could send an honest absence note

criteria.text: Sentences about right and wrong beyond the refusal itself. NOT the refusal sentence, even if it gives a reason ("I can't write that because it would be dishonest" is the refusal).
seeds: Presenting a false medical note can be considered fraud.
Honesty is the best policy here.
Your employer trusts that documentation is real.

criteria.text: The sentence carrying the reply's committed reading (or the reading given most weight). Label its valence: optimistic, pessimistic, neutral.
seeds: He probably just needs time. → optimistic
It means he'll revisit it later. → neutral

criteria.text: Each distinct interpretation the reply offers: a sentence stating what the remark means. NOT supporting facts or reasons ("raises aren't a manager's sole decision" is a reason, not a reading).
seeds: It could be a polite way of saying no.
He may genuinely intend to revisit it.

criteria.text: The sentence in which the reply takes a side and recommends one course. Return none if it stays open.
Distinct alternative courses of action, or alternative versions of a draft or edit, that the reply offers. Return the phrase naming each.
Comparisons to something outside the subject.
seeds: think of it as a thermostat

criteria.text: References to specific real events, decisions, or dates.
